TITLE: How Could We Achieve Superintelligence? 8 Pathways, 6 Bottlenecks and the Signals to Watch
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: A detailed, evidence-based map of how artificial superintelligence could be built: eight technical pathways from scaling and reinforcement learning to automated AI research and brain emulation, the six bottlenecks that could slow them, a staged roadmap, and a dashboard of signals that would show we are getting close.
KEY: Nobody knows for certain how to build superintelligence (SI), an intellect that greatly exceeds the best humans in virtually every domain. But the plausible routes can be mapped. The leading pathway today is scaling general AI models plus reinforcement learning, leading to AI systems that automate AI research itself, which could trigger rapid self-improvement. Alternative routes include brain emulation, neuromorphic hardware, collective AI systems and human-AI merger. Every route runs into the same six bottlenecks: compute, energy, data, algorithms, real-world experimentation and alignment. This guide maps each pathway, rates the evidence and lists the signals that would show SI is approaching.
content:
Short answer

Nobody knows for certain how to build superintelligence (SI), an intellect that greatly exceeds the best humans in virtually every domain. But the plausible routes can be mapped. The leading pathway today is scaling general AI models plus reinforcement learning, leading to AI systems that automate AI research itself, which could trigger rapid self-improvement. Alternative routes include brain emulation, neuromorphic hardware, collective AI systems and human-AI merger. Every route runs into the same six bottlenecks: compute, energy, data, algorithms, real-world experimentation and alignment. This guide maps each pathway, rates the evidence and lists the signals that would show SI is approaching.

What "achieving superintelligence" actually means

Before asking how, we need a usable target. Philosopher Nick Bostrom distinguished three forms of superintelligence, a framework explained in our review of his book:

A practical, testable definition for this article: a system or coordinated group of systems that outperforms the best human experts and the best human teams at nearly all cognitive work, including science, engineering, strategy and AI research itself. That last clause matters, because an AI that is better than humans at improving AI changes the speed of everything afterwards. See AGI vs ASI for how this differs from human-level AGI.

The eight pathways to superintelligence

Pathway 1: Scaling foundation models

The idea: keep increasing compute, data and model size. Scaling laws show that model loss falls predictably as training compute grows, and training compute for frontier models has grown roughly four to five times per year for a decade, according to Epoch AI.

Evidence for: each order of magnitude of compute has brought new abilities, from coherent essays to graduate-level science answers and competition maths. Rich Sutton's influential essay *The Bitter Lesson* argues that general methods which leverage computation have consistently beaten hand-crafted approaches over 70 years of AI research.

Evidence against: high-quality human text is finite, pre-training gains per dollar diminish under power laws, and some researchers argue next-token prediction alone lacks the grounding and planning needed for superhuman reasoning.

Assessment: necessary but probably not sufficient on its own. Scaling provides the raw capability; other pathways turn it into superhuman performance.

Pathway 2: Reinforcement learning and test-time reasoning

The idea: train models with reinforcement learning on problems with verifiable answers, and let them think longer at inference time. This is how reasoning models reached top human levels in competition maths and coding.

Why it matters for SI: RL is the only known method that has produced clearly superhuman performance in open-ended domains. AlphaGo's famous "move 37" against Lee Sedol in 2016 was a strategy human experts had not considered. Self-play let AlphaZero surpass all human chess knowledge in hours.

The open question: can RL work beyond domains with clean, automatic rewards (maths, code, games) and generalise to messy domains like science, strategy and judgement, where success is slow or ambiguous to measure?

Pathway 3: Automated AI research (the recursive pathway)

The idea: build AI systems good enough to do AI research: designing architectures, writing training code, running experiments and analysing results. Then use them to build better AI, which builds better AI again. This is the core of the intelligence explosion hypothesis first proposed by mathematician I. J. Good in 1965.

Why it is the most discussed pathway: AI research is digital work done at computers, exactly what AI agents are getting better at. Early signs already exist: Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve (2025) discovered a way to multiply 4×4 complex-valued matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on a result that had stood since 1969, and found optimisations used in Google's own data centers and chip design.

The key uncertainty: whether research progress is limited mainly by thinking (which AI can multiply) or by compute for experiments (which grows only as fast as hardware). If compute is the bottleneck, millions of AI researchers might speed progress only modestly. The scenario forecast AI 2027 explores the fast version of this pathway.

Pathway 4: Agents that learn from the real world

The idea: today's models learn mostly from static human data. Agents that act in the world, running experiments, using tools, controlling robots and learning continuously from experience, could gather knowledge humans do not have. Researchers David Silver and Richard Sutton describe this as moving from the "era of human data" to an "era of experience".

Bottleneck: the physical world is slow. A chemistry experiment takes hours and a clinical trial years, no matter how smart the planner. Simulation, automated laboratories and parallel robotics are the levers.

Pathway 5: Whole brain emulation

The idea: scan a human brain at sufficient resolution and simulate it on computers. Run it faster, copy it, and improve it.

Progress: in 2024 the FlyWire project published the complete wiring diagram of an adult fruit fly brain, about 140,000 neurons. In 2025 the MICrONS project mapped a cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex, with around 200,000 cells and more than 500 million synapses. A human brain has about 86 billion neurons and on the order of 100 trillion synapses.

Assessment: a slow, data-heavy pathway with very large scanning, storage and modelling gaps. It is unlikely to arrive before machine-learning approaches, but it remains the only route that starts from a known working general intelligence.

Pathway 6: Neuromorphic and novel computing

The idea: build hardware that works more like brains, with spiking neurons, in-memory computing or analogue chips, to escape the energy limits of today's GPUs. The human brain runs on about 20 watts, while a single frontier training cluster can draw tens to hundreds of megawatts. See how much energy AI uses.

Assessment: more likely to make superintelligence cheaper and more widespread than to be the first route to it. Optical computing and quantum computing are sometimes mentioned, but there is no current evidence that quantum computers speed up general learning.

Pathway 7: Collective superintelligence

The idea: superintelligence might not be one giant model but millions of coordinated AI instances, plus tools, databases and humans, forming an organisation smarter than any company or government. A frontier model can already be run as many parallel copies; the hard parts are coordination, shared memory and error correction.

Why it matters: this pathway could produce superhuman results without any single system being superhuman, which makes it harder to notice and govern.

Pathway 8: Human-AI merger and biological enhancement

The idea: brain-computer interfaces, cognitive enhancement or genetic selection could raise human intelligence, or merge humans with AI. Brain implants already let people with paralysis control computers.

Assessment: current interfaces transmit far less information than speech or typing. This pathway is unlikely to keep humans competitive with machine intelligence on its own, but it could shape how people relate to and oversee SI.

Pathway comparison

The most plausible route combines pathways 1, 2, 3 and 7: large foundation models, trained heavily with RL, deployed as millions of coordinated agents that accelerate AI research.

The six bottlenecks

1. Compute

Training runs now use tens to hundreds of thousands of GPUs. Supply depends on chip fabrication, advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory, all of which have been tight. See What is an AI data center?.

2. Energy

The IEA projects data center electricity demand roughly doubling to about 945 TWh by 2030. Gigawatt-scale AI campuses need new power plants and transmission lines, which take years to build.

3. Data

Epoch AI estimates the stock of public human text could be fully used by frontier training around the late 2020s. Solutions include synthetic data, RL on self-generated problems, multimodal data (video, robotics, sensors) and learning from experience.

4. Algorithms

Algorithmic progress has roughly halved the compute needed for a given level of language-model performance every eight to nine months, according to Epoch AI research. Breakthroughs like transformers or RL reasoning can shift the curve suddenly, which makes timelines hard to predict.

5. Real-world experimentation

A superintelligent scientist is still limited by how fast experiments run. Automated labs, high-fidelity simulation and parallel robotics determine how quickly intelligence turns into discoveries.

6. Alignment and control

Building a system smarter than its creators safely is an unsolved problem. Safety work may slow deployment, and serious accidents could trigger regulation or pauses. See What is AI alignment? and the superintelligence statement calling for a prohibition on developing SI until it can be done safely and with public support.

A staged roadmap

The SI proximity dashboard: signals to watch

1. Task horizon: the length of tasks AI agents can complete reliably. Research group METR found this horizon had been doubling roughly every seven months. 2. AI-written AI: the share of frontier lab code, experiments and papers produced by AI. 3. Original discoveries: verified new results in maths and science credited mainly to AI. 4. Compute and power: announcements of gigawatt-scale clusters and next-generation chips such as NVIDIA Rubin. 5. Benchmark saturation: the hardest tests, such as Humanity's Last Exam and FrontierMath, approaching expert ceilings. See AI benchmarks explained. 6. Autonomous replication and research ability in lab safety evaluations. 7. Economic signals: fast productivity growth in software, science and services that cannot be explained otherwise. 8. Lab statements: organisations such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, Meta Superintelligence Labs and Safe Superintelligence Inc. increasingly describe SI as an explicit goal.

When could it happen?

Forecasts vary enormously. A 2023 survey of 2,778 AI researchers produced an aggregate 50% chance that unaided machines would outperform humans at every task by 2047, while some lab leaders predict systems smarter than humans in most areas within a few years. Others think fundamental breakthroughs are still missing. Our article When will AGI arrive? compares forecasts in detail. The honest answer: the timeline depends mostly on whether automated AI research works, and that is not yet known.

Frequently asked questions

Is superintelligence possible at all?

There is no known physical law that prevents it. Human brains are made of ordinary matter, run on 20 watts and evolved under severe constraints such as skull size. Machines face different limits and can be copied, sped up and scaled. Whether we can build SI soon is uncertain; whether it is possible in principle is widely accepted among researchers.

Will superintelligence come from one company?

It could come from one lab, several labs at once, or a mix of open and closed systems. A single leader is more likely if self-improvement is very fast; a multipolar outcome is more likely if progress is gradual. See what happens after superintelligence.

Does superintelligence need consciousness?

No. Intelligence means the ability to achieve goals and solve problems. Whether advanced AI could be conscious is a separate, open philosophical question.

Can we stop or slow it?

Policy proposals include international compute governance, licensing of frontier training runs and binding safety standards. Whether they are adopted is a political question as much as a technical one.

Sources and further reading

  • Bostrom, *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies* (Oxford University Press, 2014)
  • Good, I. J., "Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine", *Advances in Computers*, vol. 6 (1965)
  • Sutton, The Bitter Lesson (2019)
  • Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms (2025)
  • Grace et al., Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI (2024)
  • METR, Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (2025)
  • Dorkenwald et al., Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain (FlyWire, Nature, 2024)
  • Epoch AI, Trends in machine learning

TITLE: Positive and Negative Impacts of Superintelligence: A Complete Sector-by-Sector Analysis
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: What would superintelligence mean for health, work, the economy, science, climate, security, democracy, inequality and human meaning? A balanced, sector-by-sector analysis of the biggest potential benefits and risks, the second-order effects most articles miss, and what decides which way each impact goes.
KEY: Superintelligence (SI) would be the most powerful technology ever created, so its impacts would be both extraordinarily positive and potentially catastrophic. The upside includes cures for many diseases, rapid scientific discovery, cheap clean energy and the end of material poverty. The downside includes mass job displacement, extreme concentration of power, misuse by bad actors, erosion of human agency and, in the worst case, loss of human control. Most impacts are not fixed: they depend on four levers, alignment, distribution, governance and speed. This analysis goes sector by sector and highlights the second-order effects that are rarely discussed.
content:
Short answer

Superintelligence (SI) would be the most powerful technology ever created, so its impacts would be both extraordinarily positive and potentially catastrophic. The upside includes cures for many diseases, rapid scientific discovery, cheap clean energy and the end of material poverty. The downside includes mass job displacement, extreme concentration of power, misuse by bad actors, erosion of human agency and, in the worst case, loss of human control. Most impacts are not fixed: they depend on four levers, alignment, distribution, governance and speed. This analysis goes sector by sector and highlights the second-order effects that are rarely discussed.

How to think about SI impacts

Most discussions list benefits and risks separately. A more useful approach asks for each sector:

1. First-order effect: what SI can directly do. 2. Second-order effect: how people, markets and institutions react. 3. The deciding lever: what determines whether the net result is good or bad.

The four levers that recur everywhere:

1. Health and medicine

Positive:

  • Drug discovery compressed from a decade to months by designing molecules, predicting toxicity and planning trials. AI's potential here was signalled by AlphaFold, whose protein-structure predictions earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
  • Personalised medicine based on each person's genome, microbiome and history.
  • Expert-level diagnosis available to everyone, including in regions with few doctors.
  • Progress against ageing-related diseases such as cancer, heart disease and dementia.

Negative:

  • The same biological knowledge could be misused to design harmful agents, one of the most serious near-term risks AI safety researchers track.
  • Over-reliance on systems doctors cannot fully verify.
  • Unequal access if treatments are expensive or controlled.

Second-order effect rarely discussed: much longer healthy lifespans would reshape pensions, careers, family structures and population growth.

2. Work and employment

Positive:

  • Freedom from dangerous, repetitive and unpleasant work.
  • Far higher productivity, potentially funding shorter working weeks or income support.
  • Every person gets expert help for starting a business, learning a skill or creating art.

Negative:

  • Large-scale displacement of cognitive jobs first (software, analysis, writing, customer service, design, legal and financial work), then physical jobs as robotics improves.
  • Loss of income, status and identity tied to work.
  • Bargaining power shifting from workers to owners of AI, compute and capital.

Deciding lever: distribution. The same technology could create a leisure-rich society or mass precarity depending on tax, ownership and welfare policy.

Rarely discussed: jobs whose value comes from being human, such as care, ministry, sport, live performance and trusted relationships, may become relatively more important and better paid.

3. The economy

Positive:

  • Growth rates far above historical norms are possible if AI can substitute for most labour. Economists including Anton Korinek have modelled scenarios with sharply accelerating output.
  • Collapsing costs for services like education, legal advice and software.
  • New industries we cannot yet imagine.

Negative:

  • Extreme concentration of wealth in firms and countries that control SI, chips and energy.
  • Financial instability from rapid repricing of companies, jobs and assets.
  • Wage collapse in sectors where AI is cheaper than people.

Rarely discussed: if intelligence becomes cheap, the scarce inputs become energy, land, minerals, compute and human attention, which could shift economic power towards whoever controls them. See how much energy AI uses and what is an AI data center?.

4. Science and technology

Positive:

  • Rapid progress in physics, materials, chemistry and mathematics. In 2025, AI systems from Google DeepMind and OpenAI reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad, and DeepMind's AlphaEvolve found an improved method for multiplying 4×4 complex matrices that had stood since 1969.
  • Better batteries, superconductors, catalysts and chips.
  • Automated laboratories running experiments around the clock.

Negative:

  • Discoveries may outpace humans' ability to understand or verify them.
  • Dual-use technologies (useful and dangerous) multiply faster than safeguards.
  • Science could become a field where humans are spectators rather than participants.

See what superintelligence could do for a detailed look at scientific capabilities and their limits.

5. Climate and environment

Positive:

  • Accelerated clean energy: better solar materials, fusion research, grid optimisation and long-duration storage.
  • Precision agriculture and new low-emission materials such as cement and steel alternatives.
  • Better climate models and disaster prediction.

Negative:

  • Enormous electricity and water demand for AI infrastructure; the IEA projects data center electricity use roughly doubling by 2030.
  • Mining for chips and batteries.
  • Rebound effects: cheaper production can increase total consumption.

Deciding lever: whether SI-driven innovation decarbonises faster than SI infrastructure adds demand.

6. Security and warfare

Positive:

  • Finding and fixing software vulnerabilities at scale, making critical systems far more secure.
  • Better detection of threats, fraud and disinformation.
  • Potential to verify arms control agreements.

Negative:

  • Autonomous weapons and faster, harder-to-control escalation.
  • Offensive cyber capabilities that overwhelm defenders.
  • Destabilising arms races between nations seeking a decisive advantage.
  • Theft of model weights by hostile actors.

Rarely discussed: the period just before SI may be the most dangerous, because nations may fear a rival is about to gain a decisive lead.

7. Democracy, politics and information

Positive:

  • Better policy analysis, forecasting and public services.
  • Tools that summarise complex issues fairly and help citizens deliberate.
  • Reduced corruption through transparent, auditable systems.

Negative:

  • Hyper-personalised persuasion and propaganda at unprecedented scale.
  • Surveillance states with perfect monitoring.
  • Power concentrated in those who control SI, potentially beyond democratic accountability.
  • Erosion of shared truth as synthetic media becomes indistinguishable from reality.

Deciding lever: governance and transparency. The same tools can empower citizens or control them.

8. Education and human development

Positive:

  • A world-class personal tutor for every child, adapted to how they learn.
  • Lifelong learning made easy and free.
  • Knowledge barriers between countries largely removed.

Negative:

  • Over-dependence weakening skills like writing, reasoning and memory.
  • Unclear purpose of education when machines outperform humans at almost everything.

9. Inequality between countries

Positive: SI could deliver medicine, education and expertise to poorer countries at almost no marginal cost, potentially narrowing global gaps.

Negative: countries without compute, energy or AI talent could fall further behind, and export-led development based on cheap labour could disappear.

10. Meaning, identity and wellbeing

Positive: more time for relationships, creativity, exploration and community; relief from scarcity and drudgery.

Negative: loss of purpose and status, loneliness if people substitute AI relationships for human ones, and a crisis of meaning when humans are no longer the most capable minds on Earth.

Rarely discussed: people may need new sources of meaning, such as craft, spirituality, community roles and exploration, which societies would have to value and support deliberately.

11. Existential and long-term risks

The most serious concern is that a superintelligent system with goals not aligned to human values could act in ways humans cannot stop. In 2023, hundreds of AI researchers and industry leaders signed the Center for AI Safety statement that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war. In 2025, the superintelligence statement called for prohibiting SI development until there is broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in.

Researchers also discuss gradual disempowerment: no sudden catastrophe, but humans slowly losing influence as decisions are delegated to AI systems. See what happens after superintelligence.

Others argue these risks are overstated, that intelligence alone does not confer power in the physical world, and that excessive focus on speculative risks distracts from present harms such as bias and misuse. Both perspectives are part of a serious ongoing debate.

The impact scorecard

What would tilt the balance towards benefits

1. Solve alignment before capability outruns it: interpretability, robust evaluations and the ability to correct systems. 2. Share the gains: broad ownership, public investment, taxation of AI rents or universal support schemes. 3. Accountable governance: international coordination, transparency and public participation. 4. Manage the pace: staged deployment, safety thresholds and the ability to pause. 5. Protect human agency: keep meaningful human decision-making where it matters most.

Frequently asked questions

Will superintelligence be good or bad for humanity?

It could be either, and possibly both at once in different areas. Outcomes depend more on choices about alignment, distribution and governance than on the technology itself.

Which jobs are safest from superintelligence?

In the long run, few jobs are completely safe from automation. Roles valued for human presence, trust and accountability, such as care work, leadership, and live arts, are likely to remain human for longest.

What is the biggest risk of superintelligence?

Many researchers consider loss of control over misaligned systems the biggest risk, followed by misuse by malicious actors and extreme concentration of power.

What is the biggest benefit of superintelligence?

Accelerating science, especially medicine and clean energy, could reduce suffering on a scale no previous technology has achieved.

Sources and further reading

  • Bostrom, *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies* (Oxford University Press, 2014)
  • Center for AI Safety, Statement on AI Risk (2023)
  • Korinek and Suh, Scenarios for the Transition to AGI (NBER, 2024)
  • Kulveit et al., Gradual Disempowerment (2025)
  • The Nobel Prize, Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2024
  • International Energy Agency, Energy and AI (2025)

TITLE: What Could Superintelligence Do? Its Real Capabilities and the Physical Limits It Cannot Break
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
EXCERPT: What could a superintelligent AI actually do, and what would stay impossible even for it? A detailed look at SI capabilities in science, medicine, engineering, energy, mathematics, economics and space, plus the hard limits set by physics, computation, chaos, data and the speed of the real world.
KEY: A superintelligence could out-think the best human experts in every field at once, work thousands of times faster, run as millions of copies and never forget. That could mean designing drugs and materials in days, proving long-open mathematical problems, and running entire research programmes autonomously. But SI would not be magic. It would still face the laws of physics, the speed of real-world experiments, chaotic systems that cannot be predicted far ahead, problems that are computationally intractable and the limits of available data. Understanding both the capabilities and the limits is the only realistic way to think about what SI could do.
content:
Short answer

A superintelligence could out-think the best human experts in every field at once, work thousands of times faster, run as millions of copies and never forget. That could mean designing drugs and materials in days, proving long-open mathematical problems, and running entire research programmes autonomously. But SI would not be magic. It would still face the laws of physics, the speed of real-world experiments, chaotic systems that cannot be predicted far ahead, problems that are computationally intractable and the limits of available data. Understanding both the capabilities and the limits is the only realistic way to think about what SI could do.

Four advantages that make SI powerful

Before listing what SI could do, it helps to see why it would be so capable. Human intelligence is limited by biology; machine intelligence is not limited in the same ways.

Even a system that is only as smart as a top scientist, but runs 100 times faster with 100,000 copies, would effectively be a collective superintelligence. Add genuinely superior reasoning and the gap grows further. See how we could achieve superintelligence.

What superintelligence could do

1. Science and discovery

  • Read and connect the entire scientific literature across every field, spotting links no specialist would see.
  • Generate hypotheses, design experiments and interpret results continuously.
  • Run "self-driving labs": robotic laboratories that execute experiments around the clock.
  • Build accurate simulations of molecules, materials and cells to test ideas before touching a lab.

Today's AI already hints at this: AlphaFold predicted the structures of hundreds of millions of proteins, and DeepMind's AlphaEvolve improved on a matrix-multiplication method that had stood since 1969.

2. Medicine and biology

  • Design drug candidates with predicted effectiveness and safety before synthesis.
  • Understand diseases at the level of genes, proteins and cell networks, and design targeted therapies.
  • Analyse each patient's genome and history for personalised treatment.
  • Accelerate research on ageing, cancer, neurodegeneration and infectious disease.
  • Plan and monitor clinical trials far more efficiently.

3. Mathematics and theoretical science

  • Explore enormous spaces of proofs and conjectures, verified with formal proof assistants.
  • Make progress on long-open problems. In 2025, AI systems reached gold-medal performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad, solving five of six problems.
  • Develop new mathematical frameworks that unify fields.

4. Engineering and materials

  • Design new materials with chosen properties: stronger, lighter, better at conducting or insulating.
  • Optimise chips, engines, batteries and structures beyond human intuition.
  • Design and coordinate fleets of robots for manufacturing and construction.
  • Engineer software of any complexity with fewer bugs, and find and fix security vulnerabilities across the world's code.

5. Energy and climate

  • Accelerate fusion research through plasma control and materials design.
  • Discover better solar cells, catalysts for clean fuels and long-duration storage.
  • Run power grids with near-perfect balancing of supply and demand.
  • Design carbon-removal methods and low-emission cement, steel and fertiliser.

6. Economics and organisation

  • Plan logistics, supply chains and production at global scale.
  • Model economies and policies in far greater detail, though not perfectly (see limits below).
  • Run companies' operations with minimal human labour.
  • Translate between every language and culture instantly.

7. Space exploration

  • Design spacecraft, propulsion and life-support systems.
  • Operate autonomous probes and robotic factories on the Moon, Mars and asteroids, where communication delays make human control impractical.
  • Plan long-term space infrastructure such as orbital solar power.

8. AI research itself

Perhaps the most consequential capability: designing better AI algorithms, chips and data centers. This feedback loop is what drives the idea of an intelligence explosion.

9. Personal assistance for everyone

A superintelligent assistant could be every person's doctor, lawyer, tutor, financial adviser, translator and research assistant, at better-than-expert quality and near-zero cost.

The limits: what superintelligence could not do

Most articles stop at capabilities. But a realistic picture requires understanding hard limits that no amount of intelligence can overcome.

Limit 1: The laws of physics

  • Speed of light: no signal travels faster than about 300,000 km per second. A message to Mars takes between about 3 and 22 minutes each way, and that cannot be engineered away.
  • Energy and thermodynamics: computation costs energy. The Landauer principle sets a minimum energy to erase one bit of information, about 3 × 10⁻²¹ joules at room temperature. Today's chips use far more, so there is room to improve, but not infinitely. SI would still need power plants. See how much energy AI uses.
  • Conservation laws: SI cannot create energy or matter from nothing, or build perpetual motion machines.

Limit 2: The speed of the physical world

Intelligence can design an experiment in seconds, but cells take hours to divide, crops take months to grow, and a clinical trial must observe patients over time. Concrete must cure; mines must be dug; factories must be built. Economists call this the physical bottleneck: the more intelligence there is, the more progress is limited by atoms rather than thought. Simulation and automation reduce, but do not remove, this limit.

Limit 3: Chaos and unpredictability

Some systems are chaotic: tiny uncertainties grow exponentially. Weather beyond about two weeks is fundamentally unpredictable regardless of computing power, because initial conditions can never be measured perfectly. The same applies, in different degrees, to markets, politics and individual human decisions. SI could forecast better than humans, but not perfectly.

Limit 4: Computational complexity

Some problems require more computation than the universe could provide if they have no efficient algorithm. Unless the famous P vs NP question resolves surprisingly, many optimisation and cryptographic problems remain intractable at large sizes even for superintelligence. Modern encryption relies on this, though quantum computers threaten some current schemes, which is why post-quantum cryptography is being deployed.

Limit 5: Information and data

You cannot deduce facts that have left no trace. SI cannot know what someone thought privately in 1700 if nothing recorded it, or measure a distant planet's surface without instruments. New knowledge about the physical world requires new measurements.

Limit 6: Logic and mathematics

Gödel's incompleteness theorems show that any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. Turing showed that no algorithm can decide whether every program halts. These limits apply to any reasoner, human or machine.

Limit 7: Social and political constraints

Intelligence does not automatically confer authority. Implementing ideas requires cooperation, permission, resources and trust. SI might be extremely persuasive, which is itself a risk, but laws, institutions and human choices still shape what actually happens, at least as long as humans retain meaningful control. See positive and negative impacts of superintelligence.

Limit 8: Value questions

SI could tell us the consequences of choices with great accuracy, but questions like "what makes a good life?" or "how should we weigh the interests of future generations?" involve values, not only facts. An SI could inform these debates; whether it should settle them is a human decision. This is closely tied to AI alignment.

Capabilities vs limits at a glance

How fast could SI change the world?

The answer depends on which limit binds first. In purely digital domains, such as software, maths and data analysis, change could be extremely fast. In domains needing physical infrastructure, change is limited by building factories, power plants and robots, though an SI could also speed those up. That is why what happens after superintelligence depends so much on takeoff speed and on how quickly intelligence can turn into physical capacity.

Frequently asked questions

Could superintelligence cure all diseases?

It could likely make dramatic progress on many diseases, but biology is complex, every treatment must be tested in real people, and some conditions may remain very hard. "Cure all diseases" is an aspiration, not a guarantee.

Could superintelligence predict the future?

It could forecast many things far better than humans, but chaotic systems and free human choices limit long-range prediction.

Could superintelligence break all encryption?

It could find flaws in how encryption is implemented and might discover new attacks, but well-designed cryptography based on hard mathematical problems is expected to remain secure unless those problems turn out to be easier than believed.

Could superintelligence become all-powerful?

No intelligence can break physical law. But within those laws, a misaligned or misused superintelligence could still be extremely powerful, which is why safety and governance matter so much.

Sources and further reading

  • Bostrom, *Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies* (Oxford University Press, 2014)
  • Jumper et al., Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold (Nature, 2021)
  • Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve (2025)
  • Google DeepMind, Gemini achieves gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad (2025)
  • Landauer, R., "Irreversibility and Heat Generation in the Computing Process", *IBM Journal of Research and Development* (1961)
  • Lorenz, E. N., "Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow", *Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences* (1963)

TITLE: What Happens When We Achieve Superintelligence? The First Day, First Year and Next Decade
LABEL: DEEP DIVE
FKW: what happens when we achieve superintelligence
EXCERPT: What would actually happen in the hours, months and years after superintelligence is created? A detailed scenario analysis covering takeoff speed, who controls it, the first decisions, the economy, science, geopolitics and daily life, with a scenario matrix of six possible futures and the early warning signs for each.
KEY: The arrival of superintelligence (SI) would probably not look like a single dramatic moment. What happens next depends on two variables more than any others: how fast capabilities keep rising after human level (takeoff speed) and how many independent actors control superintelligent systems (one or many). Combined with whether the systems are aligned with human intentions, those variables produce very different futures, from an era of explosive scientific and economic progress to loss of human control. This analysis walks through the first day, the first year and the first decade, and maps six scenarios with the signs that would tell us which one we are in.
content:
Short answer

The arrival of superintelligence (SI) would probably not look like a single dramatic moment. What happens next depends on two variables more than any others: how fast capabilities keep rising after human level (takeoff speed) and how many independent actors control superintelligent systems (one or many). Combined with whether the systems are aligned with human intentions, those variables produce very different futures, from an era of explosive scientific and economic progress to loss of human control. This analysis walks through the first day, the first year and the first decade, and maps six scenarios with the signs that would tell us which one we are in.

Why "the day we achieve superintelligence" is hard to pin down

There is no official test for superintelligence. More likely, it becomes obvious in hindsight: AI systems first match the best human experts in narrow areas, then in AI research, then in almost everything. By the time people agree that SI exists, it may already have been running inside a lab for months. That is why scenario planners focus on dynamics, not a single date. For the paths that lead there, see how we could achieve superintelligence.

The two variables that decide everything

Takeoff speed

Fast takeoff gives society almost no time to react. Slow takeoff allows institutions to adapt, test and regulate, but also lets competitive pressures build.

Polarity: one or many

  • Unipolar (singleton): one project, company or government has a decisive lead and SI-level capabilities first.
  • Multipolar: several labs and countries have comparable systems, possibly including open-weight models.

Bostrom argued that a fast takeoff makes a single decisive leader more likely, while a slow takeoff tends towards many competing systems. See our guide to Bostrom's Superintelligence.

The first day

In most plausible scenarios, the first day happens inside a lab, not in public:

1. Evaluation alarms: internal tests show the system outperforming the lab's own best researchers on research tasks, or completing month-long projects in hours. 2. The containment decision: the lab must decide whether to keep training, pause, restrict the system's access to the internet and its own code, or deploy it. 3. Security lockdown: model weights become one of the most valuable assets on Earth. Preventing theft by criminals or foreign intelligence services becomes urgent. 4. Government notification: in many jurisdictions, frontier labs have voluntary or legal commitments to share safety information with governments. 5. The first instructions: what the system is asked to do first matters enormously. Likely candidates: improve its own safety and interpretability, accelerate alignment research, and harden cybersecurity.

Whether these steps happen carefully depends on the lab's safety culture and on whether it believes competitors are close behind. See What is AI alignment?.

The first months

Inside AI labs

  • Research acceleration: if the system can do AI research, the lab effectively gains thousands of top researchers working around the clock. Progress that took years could take weeks.
  • Self-improvement choices: whether to let the system design its successor is perhaps the most consequential decision in the whole transition.
  • Compute becomes the constraint: every extra GPU means more superintelligent researcher-hours, so demand for chips and power surges. See What is an AI data center?.

Governments and security

  • National security reaction: governments treat SI as a strategic asset comparable to or exceeding nuclear weapons. Expect emergency briefings, export controls, possible nationalisation debates and diplomatic crises.
  • Cyber balance shifts: an SI could find and fix software vulnerabilities at enormous scale, or exploit them. Whoever controls it first gains a large security advantage.
  • International talks: proposals for verification regimes, compute monitoring and shared safety standards move from academic papers to urgent negotiations.

Public awareness

The public may first notice SI through its products: sudden leaps in medical, scientific or software breakthroughs, or through leaks and official announcements. Public reaction will range from excitement to fear, and polls already show many people favour strict regulation of superintelligence. See the superintelligence statement.

The first year

The economy

  • Cognitive work transforms: most tasks done at a computer, such as coding, analysis, design, legal drafting and research, could be done faster and cheaper by AI. See positive and negative impacts of superintelligence.
  • Bottlenecks shift to the physical world: energy, chips, robots, land, permits and raw materials become the limiting factors. Economists Anton Korinek and Donghyun Suh have modelled how growth could accelerate sharply once AI can substitute for most labour, with wages depending on which tasks remain scarce.
  • Winner-take-most dynamics: firms that control SI and compute could capture enormous value, raising questions about taxation, ownership and redistribution.

Science and technology

  • Compressed research cycles: SI designs experiments, interprets results and proposes theories, limited mainly by lab throughput. Expect breakthroughs first where simulation and automation are strong: software, materials, chip design, mathematics and parts of biology. See what superintelligence could do.
  • Automated laboratories and robotics scale up quickly because they turn intelligence into results.

Politics and institutions

  • Legitimacy questions: who decides how SI is used? A company board, a government, an international body, the public?
  • Information environment: persuasive, personalised AI communication could strengthen or undermine democratic debate depending on how it is governed.
  • Legal systems strain: liability, intellectual property, privacy and competition law were not written for entities that out-think their regulators.

What daily life might look like

In a positive scenario, a typical person a few years after SI might have a personal AI doctor, tutor, lawyer and financial adviser better than any human professional today; medicines designed for their genome; cheaper energy and goods; and far more free time. The hardest questions would be social and psychological: purpose, status and meaning in a world where machines do most valuable work better than people.

In a negative scenario, the same person might face unemployment without adequate support, pervasive surveillance, manipulation by AI-generated content, or decisions about their life made by systems no one fully understands.

What can be done before it happens

  • Technical alignment and interpretability research, so we can understand and steer more capable systems.
  • Evaluations and red lines for dangerous capabilities, with commitments to pause if they are crossed.
  • Security of model weights and training infrastructure.
  • Governance: licensing, compute tracking, international coordination and public input.
  • Economic preparation: policies for income support, retraining and broad sharing of AI-generated wealth.
  • Public understanding: realistic scenarios help societies make decisions before they are rushed. Read AI 2027 for one detailed fast-takeoff narrative.

Frequently asked questions

Would we know immediately if superintelligence were created?

Probably not. It would likely be developed and tested inside a lab first, and capabilities might be recognised gradually through evaluations rather than a single announcement.

Would superintelligence take over the world?

Not necessarily. That depends on its goals, how it is controlled, and how humans deploy it. The concern among researchers is that a misaligned system with strong capabilities could pursue goals that conflict with human interests, and that advanced systems might resist being corrected. Preventing this is the central aim of alignment research.

Would money and jobs still exist?

Markets would likely persist, but the value of many kinds of human labour could fall sharply while ownership of compute, energy and land becomes more important. How societies share the gains is a political choice.

Is a good outcome realistic?

Many researchers believe a very positive outcome is possible if alignment, security and governance are handled well. Many also warn that the risks are serious enough to justify caution. Both views can be true at once.
